title: Parsing with a stack
objectives: Evaluate and decode nested expressions with a stack.

screens.title: Two stacks
screens.prose: In `ds/l9-last-in-first-out` you evaluated postfix with one stack. Ordinary infix needs two: one for numbers and one for operators. Here `4+3*2` has been read to the end, and nothing has been applied yet.
screens.question: What is the value of `4+3*2`?

hints.text: Which operator binds tighter?
`*` sits on top of the operator stack. It comes off first.
Apply `*` to 3 and 2, giving 6. Then apply `+` to 4 and 6.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiplication comes before addition.

byKey.ltr: You worked left to right: $4 + 3 = 7$, then $7 \times 2$. `*` binds tighter, so it goes first.

explain.text: `*` binds tighter than `+`, so it waits on top and comes off first. The stacks turn `4+3*2` into $4 + (3 \times 2) = 10$. Reading left to right gives 14, which is wrong.

screens.title: Run the parser
screens.prose: Step through `4+3*2` one token at a time. A number goes on its stack. An operator first applies any waiting operator that binds at least as tightly. At the end, apply what is left.
screens.question: Run the parser to the end of `4+3*2`.

ops.label: Apply + first
ops.why: `+` binds less tightly than `*`, so it waits. Only operators that bind at least as tightly as `*` come off.

ops.label: Apply +
ops.why: Only the top of a stack comes off. `*` is on top, so it goes first.

hints.text: Push numbers as they come. When does an operator wait?
When `*` arrives, `+` is on top. `+` binds less tightly, so it stays.
Push 4, push `+`, push 3, push `*`, push 2. Then apply `*` and then `+`.

feedback.correct: The stacks ended with one number, 10.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. An operator comes off only from the top, and only when the incoming one binds no more tightly.

explain.text: The applies came out as `*` then `+`. That is the postfix form `4 3 2 * +`, which you evaluated in `ds/l9-last-in-first-out`. The operator stack turns infix into that order as it reads.

screens.title: Equal ranks
screens.prose: Now `10-2-3`. The parser has read `10-2`, and the second `-` arrives. Both minus signs have the same rank.
screens.question: What should the parser do before it pushes the second `-`?

options.text: Apply the waiting `-` first, giving 8, so the result is 5
Push it on top and apply both at the end, giving 11
options.why: You let the later minus go first: $10 - (2 - 3) = 11$. Equal ranks apply left to right, so the waiting one comes off.

options.text: Either order: subtraction gives the same answer

options.why: The second `-` has no right operand yet. Only the waiting one can be applied.

hints.text: The waiting `-` is on top of the operator stack.
Use `>=`: pop while the top binds at least as tightly. So the waiting `-` comes off and 8 is pushed.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Equal ranks are applied left to right.

byKey.b: You let the later minus go first. That computes $10 - (2 - 3) = 11$.
byKey.c: You treated subtraction like addition. Moving the brackets changes a difference.
byKey.d: You tried to apply the incoming `-`, which has no right operand yet.

explain.text: The loop pops while the top binds at least as tightly, with `>=`. With `>` the second minus would wait and give 11. Left to right for equal ranks is the convention the tests expect.

canvas.caption: After the first `-`: 8, then `-` goes on

screens.title: Brackets
screens.prose: A `(` goes on the operator stack and stops the popping. A `)` applies operators back to its `(` and then drops it. Run `2*(5+5*2)/3+(6/2+8)` on paper. Division here gives whole numbers.
screens.question: Fill in the value and the largest number of entries the operator stack ever holds, brackets included.

rows: Peak size of the operator stack

hints.text: Evaluate each bracket first, then the rest.
When the inner `*` arrives, the stack holds `*`, `(` and `+`. `+` binds less tightly, so `*` goes on top.
$2 \times 15 / 3 = 10$ and $6 / 2 + 8 = 11$, so 21. The stack peaks at `* ( + *`, four entries.

feedback.correct: 21, and the stack peaks at four entries: `* ( + *`.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work the brackets first, and count `(` as an entry.

byKey.r0c1: Check the value. The first bracket is 15, so $2 \times 15 / 3 = 10$; the second is $3 + 8 = 11$.
byKey.r1c1: Check the peak. After `2*(5+5`, the next `*` lands on `* ( +`, making four entries.

explain.text: The stack peaks at `* ( + *` just before the second 2 arrives. `)` then applies `*` and `+` back to the bracket, leaving 15. The value is $10 + 11 = 21$.

screens.title: Toward zero
screens.prose: The assessment says: "`/` is whole-number division that truncates toward zero." Python's `//` is close, but not the same.
screens.question: Under the statement's rule, what is `-7/2`?

hints.text: Work out $-7 / 2$ exactly first.
`//` rounds down, toward minus infinity.
$-7/2 = -3.5$. Toward zero means drop the fraction: $-3$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Truncating toward zero drops the fraction.

byKey.floor: You used floor division. `//` rounds $-3.5$ down to $-4$; the statement truncates toward zero, to $-3$.
byKey.exact: That is true division. The statement asks for a whole number, truncated toward zero.

explain.text: `//` floors: it gives −4 for −7 // 2. Truncating toward zero gives −3, which is `int(-7 / 2)` in Python and plain `/` on `int` in C++. Write it as `abs(a) // abs(b)` with the sign put back.

screens.title: Write the calculator
screens.prose: A `-` is unary when an operand is expected: at the start, after `(` and after another operator. Push it as `'u'` with the highest rank and do not pop before it, so `-(2+3)*4` and `2*-3` work.

state.caption: `-(2+3)*4` after `-(`: the minus went on as unary `u`

screens.question: Write `calculate(s)`: `s` holds whole numbers, `+ - * /`, spaces and brackets, and `-` may be unary. `/` truncates toward zero. Return an `int`.

widget.how: Check runs 15 hidden tests. The `eval` starter passes 13 of them, which is most of the marks. The two it fails are the reason for the stacks.

feedback.correct: Two stacks, a unary minus and truncating division pass all 15.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-2: Test 2 has spaces around the numbers. Skip a space and move on.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 starts with a unary minus. A `-` where an operand is expected negates what follows.
byKey.test-6: Test 6 is `-7/2`. You used floor division, which gives −4; the statement truncates toward zero, to −3.
byKey.test-7: Test 7 is `(-7)/2`. You used floor division, which gives −4; truncate toward zero instead.

screens.title: Nested repeats
screens.prose: A second parsing question: `k[text]` means `text` repeated `k` times, and brackets nest. On `[` the decoder pushes the text built so far and the count, then starts afresh. On `]` it pops them back.

state.caption: The stack just after the second `[` of `2[b3[a]]`

screens.question: How long is each decoded string?

hints.text: Decode the innermost bracket first.
`3[a]` is `aaa`, so `b3[a]` is `baaa`.
`2[b3[a]]` is `baaabaaa`, 8 letters. `3[xy]2[z]w` is `xyxyxy` + `zz` + `w`, 9 letters.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Decode from the inside out.

byKey.r0c1: Check `2[b3[a]]`. The inner part `b3[a]` is `baaa`, 4 letters, repeated twice.
byKey.r1c1: Check `3[xy]2[z]w`. That is 6 letters, then 2, then the plain `w`.

explain.text: On `]` the decoder pops `('b', 3)` and makes `'b' + 'aaa'`. The next `]` pops `('', 2)` and repeats `baaa` twice. Lengths multiply inward: $2 \times (1 + 3) = 8$.

screens.title: Write the decoder
screens.prose: A count may have several digits, as in `12[xy]`. Build it as you read: `count = count * 10 + int(ch)`. Keep the current text as a list of pieces and join it once.

state.caption: Each entry is the text before a `[` and its count

screens.question: Write `decode_string(s)`: expand every `k[text]`, with nesting and counts of several digits.

widget.how: Check runs 10 hidden tests, including an empty input, a count of 10 and an empty bracket `1[]`.

hints.text: What must you remember when a `[` opens?
The text before the `[` and the count that goes with it.
On `[` push `(cur, count)` and reset both. On `]` pop `(prev, k)`, append `''.join(cur) * k` to `prev`, and make `prev` current.

feedback.correct: The stack holds one `(text, count)` pair per open bracket.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 is `3[a]2[bc]`. Each `k[...]` repeats its text `k` times.
byKey.test-2: Test 2 nests: `2[b3[a]]`. Push the text so far on `[` and append to it on `]`.
byKey.test-5: Test 5 is `10[a]`. Build the count digit by digit: `count * 10 + int(ch)`.
byKey.test-9: Test 9 is `1[]`, an empty bracket. Repeating an empty text gives `''`.
byKey.test-10: Test 10 is `12[xy]`. A count of 12 arrives as two digits.

explain.text: Each `[` saves where you were, and each `]` resumes it with the repeat appended. The stack is as deep as the nesting. Joining a list of pieces avoids quadratic string building.

canvas.caption: `('b', 3)` comes off first, at the inner `]`

screens.title: The pattern
screens.prose:
Both parsers keep a stack of what is waiting.

```python
# evaluate: apply while the top binds at least as tightly
while ops and ops[-1] != '(' and prec[ops[-1]] >= prec[c]:
    apply()
# decode: save on '[', resume on ']'
stack.append((cur, count))
prev, k = stack.pop()
```
screens.question: Put the decoder's steps for `2[b3[a]]` in order. Leave out the step that does not belong.

lines.text: Read `2`: push the character `'2'` onto the stack
lines.why: A count of 12 would arrive as `'1'` and `'2'`, two entries. Build the number in `count` instead.

hints.text: Follow the input left to right.
Digits build `count`; they are never pushed on their own.

feedback.correct: Seven steps, one per part of the input.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow the input from left to right.

byKey.d1: You pushed the digit as a character. A count of 12 would split into 1 and 2.
byKey.left-out: Every step but one belongs. Only the push of `'2'` is wrong.

explain.text: Each `[` pushes one pair and each `]` pops one. The inner `]` finishes `baaa` before the outer one repeats it. Digits only ever build `count`.

screens.title: A formula in a config file
screens.prose: A risk system reads limits from a text file, written as formulas with brackets and minus signs. A colleague suggests `eval` on each line. Anyone who can edit the file can then type any Python.
screens.question: Which parser should the desk allow, and why?

options.text: The stack parser: `eval` would run any code in the file
`eval`: it is shorter and already understands brackets
options.why: Short is not safe. Line 3 would run code, and `eval` floors `-800/3` with `//` instead of truncating.
That changes the division and nothing else. Line 3 still runs, and `//` floors negatives.

options.text: Either: they give the same numbers
options.why: They differ on negative division, and only one of them runs arbitrary code.

hints.text: What does line 3 do under `eval`?
It imports a module and calls a function.
The stack parser rejects any character that is not a digit, an operator, a bracket or a space. `eval` runs whatever it is given.

feedback.correct: The stack parser reads arithmetic and nothing else.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about what a hostile line in the file could do.

byKey.b: You chose the shorter code. `eval` would run line 3, and it floors negative division.
byKey.c: You fixed the division sign only. Line 3 still runs as code.
byKey.d: You compared only the answers. `eval` also runs arbitrary code from the file.

explain.text: `eval` executes the text, so a line in a config file can delete files or leak data. The stack parser accepts digits, `+ - * /`, brackets and spaces, and nothing else. It also truncates as the statement asks.

screens.title: Small input, large output
screens.prose: An exchange's test feed compresses repeated messages as `k[...]`. A message of 10 characters can expand a long way. The decoder's stack holds one entry per open bracket.

state.caption: The deepest point of `9[9[9[a]]]`: three entries

screens.question: How many letters does `9[9[9[a]]]` decode to?

hints.text: Decode the innermost bracket first.
`9[a]` is 9 letters. The next bracket repeats those 9 letters 9 times.
$9 \times 9 \times 9 = 729$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each bracket multiplies the length inside it.

byKey.sum: You added the counts. Each bracket repeats everything inside it, so the counts multiply.
byKey.two: That is $9^2$. There are three brackets, so multiply by 9 three times.
byKey.depth: 3 is the depth of the stack. The question asks for the length of the output.

explain.text: Each level repeats the one inside it 9 times, so the length is $9^3 = 729$. The stack never holds more than 3 entries. Time is $O(\text{output})$, while the stack is $O(\text{depth})$.

ideas: Infix needs two stacks. Before pushing an operator, apply every waiting one that binds at least as tightly; `)` applies back to its `(`.
A `-` where an operand is expected is unary. Division that truncates toward zero is not Python's `//` for negatives.
To decode `k[text]`, push the text so far and the count on `[`. Pop them on `]` and append the repeat.
summary.trap: `//` floors, so `-7 // 2` is −4. A statement that truncates toward zero wants −3.

options.text: The text so far and the repeat count

options.why: Without the text so far, `a2[b]` would lose the `a` when the bracket closes.
Pushing the bracket itself, as in a bracket check, keeps neither the text nor the count.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. What does `]` need to finish the job?
